conversation.content:
Hello—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m so glad you’re here. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s a simple 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless safety is a concern. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to begin?

Thinking about the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, it’s been pretty hard to find anything funny lately… I’ve laughed maybe once or twice, but even then it felt forced, like I was just pretending to enjoy the moment. Most of the time I don’t really feel like laughing at all.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly it’s felt like a struggle. I can laugh here and there—maybe once or twice—but it’s like the joy fades right away and I’m back to feeling flat or sad.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get a little spark when I think about a couple of things—like the baby’s bath time or having coffee with my neighbor—but it’s nowhere near the excitement I used to feel. Most plans just feel like chores I have to get through rather than something to enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong as a mom. Even little things—like spilling a bit of milk or being late to an appointment—turn into “I’m failing at this.” It isn’t constant, but it pops into my head most days.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

That happens to me pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s fine, but my mind just races—what if he stops breathing, what if I’m not holding him right, what if the pediatrician missed something? I know there’s no real reason, but I can’t shut the worries off. Some days I can take a breath and calm down, but it keeps coming back.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart races, I feel shaky, and I have to check the baby every few seconds even though nothing’s wrong. It passes after a bit if I walk around or breathe deeply, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. The feeding, the laundry, trying to sleep—it all piles up and I think, “I can’t do this.” I haven’t had any drinks or pills to cope, but there’ve been moments I had to put the baby in the crib and just sit in the bathroom to keep from falling apart.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling through all the “what-ifs” and things I think I did wrong. It takes me forever to drift off, and when I do, I wake up at least once or twice with my heart pounding and those anxious thoughts right there again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s not tears-all-day level, but there’s this heavy, sad feeling that follows me around. I’ll be doing something normal—folding onesies or warming a bottle—and just feel empty or discouraged, like the color’s been drained out of everything.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, a couple of times this week. It’s usually when everything feels like too much—like yesterday when I couldn’t get him to latch and I just sat there in the rocker crying. The tears don’t last hours, but they come out of nowhere and leave me feeling even more wiped out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s crossed my mind once or twice in the past week. Nothing planned—just these quick, scary flashes like “what if I weren’t here?” They pass fast, but they shake me up, because I don’t ever want to leave my baby without a mom.

You've shared how most days feel heavy and colourless since your baby arrived: fleeting moments of laughter fade quickly into flat sadness, simple tasks feel overwhelming, and worries about being a "good enough" mum loop in your mind. You described sudden panicky waves that leave you checking on your son and nights spent staring at the ceiling while anxious thoughts race. Crying spells come out of nowhere, and scary, passing thoughts of not being here have shaken you. You've been coping by putting the baby down and stepping away to breathe, yet you still feel you're barely treading water.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can laugh only occasionally and joy quickly fades, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only a faint spark of enjoyment in rare moments and states most plans feel like chores, clearly indicating "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries without cause, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple discrete panic episodes this week with physical symptoms and compulsive checking, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage daily tasks, and needing to separate from the baby to avoid falling apart, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple nights of insomnia driven by persistent anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily low mood with anhedonia and emotional emptiness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Response describes multiple crying episodes triggered by feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Response indicates fleeting intrusive self-harm thoughts occurring a few times in the past week, aligning with "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring guidelines indicate scores ≥14 require urgent referral; your score of 24 is well above this threshold. <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> require ≥5 symptoms during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum: you endorse <sym>depressed mood</sym> daily, <sym>marked loss of interest</sym>, <sym>self-blame/guilt</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, and <sym>fleeting suicidal ideation</sym>, with clinically significant distress. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>GP</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for formal assessment and safety planning
2. Share these EPDS results and your description of <quote>scary flashes of not being here</quote> so they can evaluate risk and discuss treatment options such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Build a brief daily self-care plan: 10 minutes rest when baby sleeps, accept help with chores, and practice 4-7-8 breathing when panic rises
4. Identify 24-hour supports: save the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline number 1-833-943-5746 in your phone for overnight reassurance
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress after interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤12 wk post-delivery (perinatal context noted)

Presenting Symptoms (endorsed):
- Persistent low mood, “empty,” daily sadness (Q8)  
- Marked anhedonia—minimal enjoyment, activities feel like chores (Q1, Q2)  
- Daily, intrusive anxious worries; panic spells 3–4×/wk (Q4, Q5)  
- Unwarranted self-blame/guilt re parenting competence, several × week (Q3)  
- Frequent crying spells, 2× past week (Q9)  
- Sleep-onset and mid-night awakening linked to ruminative worry (Q7)  
- Overwhelm/“can’t cope,” no substance use reported (Q6)  
- Passive self-harm ideation (fleeting thoughts “what if I weren’t here”) 1–2× past week; no plan or intent (Q10)

Pattern: Symptoms present most days × ≥2 wk, interfere with functioning; no psychotic features; no current mania.

Risk Flags:
- Active passive suicidal ideation → safety concern  
- Moderate–severe anxiety with panic equivalents  
- Impaired sleep, concentration, coping

Screening Impression: High clinical likelihood of major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; rule-out generalized anxiety disorder, panic spectrum, PTSD. Immediate safety plan and formal diagnostic evaluation recommended.
